_______________________________________________________

Reasons for Judgment

of
the

Honourable Mr. Justice John J. Gill

_______________________________________________________

Summary:

[
1
]

This application raises a number
of matters in regards to the pleadings. There is an application filed by the
Defendant Najmeya Sana (“Sana”) to amend her Counterclaim and a
counter-application by the Plaintiff and the Edmonton Public School Board (the
“School Board”)  to strike the Counterclaim. The Plaintiff’s and the School
Board’s application to strike the Counterclaim is granted as the Counterclaim
(including the proposed amendments) does not disclose a cause of action and is
otherwise an abuse of process.

[
2
]

In addition, the Plaintiff’s
application to strike Sana’s affidavit dated October 13, 2006 is granted.
Sana’s applications to add the Alberta Teacher’s Association (the “ATA” ) as a
Defendant to the Counterclaim and to strike paragraphs 22 and 23 of the amended
Statement of Claim are dismissed.

Background:

[
3
]

The Plaintiff was a principal at a
school (the “school’) in Edmonton attended by Sana’s children. The Plaintiff
sued Sana and her husband Arif Sana Siddiqi for defamation in relation to
various statements allegedly made by Sana. The Plaintiff has amended her
original Statement of Claim to include further allegations concerning written
statements, letters, and notices sent by the Defendant. Sana filed a Statement
of Defence and Counterclaim and now applies to amend the Counterclaim. The
Plaintiff has applied to strike the original Counterclaim and along with the
School Board opposes the proposed amendment.

[
4
]

In the proposed amendments to the
Counterclaim additional allegations are made against the Plaintiff. Sana also
seeks to add the School Board as a Defendant by Counterclaim.
The additional allegations include the
following:

(a)        the Plaintiff owes a
professional duty of care to Sana not to act in a manner that is detrimental to
the best interests of students, the public or teaching profession;

(b)        the Plaintiff has breached this
duty of care, has behaved in a discriminatory manner and has defamed Sana;

(c)        the School Board owes a duty of
care pursuant to the
School Act
, R.S.A. 2000, c. S-3, and
Human
Rights, Citizenship and Multiculturalism Act
, R.S.A. 2000, c. H-14, not to
discriminate with regard to goods services, accommodation or facilities which
duty was breached by denying Sana access to the school and discriminating
against her;

(d)        Sana has suffered stress and
psychological problems as a result of the actions of the Plaintiff;

(e)        the Plaintiff and the School Board
defamed Sana by providing information to Children’s Services concerning Sana
and the children;

(f)        the School Board has without
justification extended a ban on Sana including all School Board property,
depriving the children and Sana of parental contact and interaction with
teachers;

(g)        that the Plaintiff and the
School Board has defamed Sana to the principals and staff at other schools
including McKernan School.

[
5
]

Sana is the subject of two bans
under
section 27
of the
School Act
. The first ban was issued by the
Plaintiff in relation to the school, and the second one issued by the School
Board relates to other schools and property controlled by the School Board.

[
6
]

Sana filed a Human Rights
complaint filed with the Alberta Human Rights and Citizenship Commission on
September 15, 2005 against the Plaintiff and the Edmonton Public School Board,
the Superintendent of Schools, the Chair and the Board of Trustees. The
complaint alleges harassment and discrimination including:

·           June 2, 2004: refers to the
section 27

notice of trespass given by the Plaintiff to Sana

·           September 16, 2004: refers to the
section
27
notice of trespass given by the Superintendent of Edmonton Public Schools to
Sana;

·           October, 2004: refers to telephone calls
by Sana to the School Board, the Plaintiff
’s Secretary, Office of the Public Trustee and the School Board’s lawyer;

·           September 29, 2004: refers to daughter
breaking her knee playing basketball and the fact that Sana could not help her
daughter;

·           February 2, 2005: refers to a call from
one of her sons who had a fever and was too weak to walk. He slipped coming out
of the school. Refers to emergencies like this where no one could help her
children;

·           June 28, 2006: refers to one of her sons’ grade 6 ceremony. Her daughter Samina was not
allowed to take pictures and was pushed by the Plaintiff towards the door;

·           Refers to one of the sons being allergic
to cats and dogs. She spoke to the Plaintiff’s secretary to ask for help to ask parents not to bring their dogs and
cats near the school entrance or grounds. The Plaintiff and School Board did
not give any help;

·           Refers to Sana not getting help despite
her physical disability and asking for help.

[
7
]

There have also been 2
complaints filed against the Plaintiff relating to the same set of
circumstances by Sana’s children pursuant to the code of professional conduct
of the ATA and the
Teaching Profession Act
, R.S.A. 2000, c. T-2.

Issues

1.         Should the amendment to the Counterclaim be
allowed and/or should the Counterclaim be struck?

2.         Should the Affidavit filed by Sana in
support of the application to amend the Counterclaim be struck?

3.         Should the ATA be added as a party to the
Counterclaim?

4.         Should
paragraphs 23 and 24 of the Amended Statement of Claim be struck?

Issue # 1.
Should the amendment to the Counterclaim be allowed and/or should the
Counterclaim be struck
?

[
8
]

The Plaintiff and the Board have
commenced an action to strike Sana’s Counterclaim. When as in this case, there
is a cross-motion to amend a counterclaim the Court should look at the proposed
amendment to see if they disclose a cause of action.

United Petroleum
Distributors Calgary Ltd. v. 548311 Alberta Ltd.

(1998),
1998 ABCA 121 (CanLII)
,
216 A.R. 116
(C.A.)
.

[
9
]

The application to strike is made
pursuant to Rule 129.

129(1)  The
court may at any stage of the proceedings order to be struck out or amended any
pleading in the action, on the ground that

(a) it discloses no cause of
action or defence, as the case may be, or

(b) it is scandalous,
frivolous or vexatious, or

(c) it may prejudice,
embarrass or delay the fair trial of the action, or

(d) it is otherwise an abuse
of the process of the court,

and may order the action to
be stayed or dismissed or judgment to be entered accordingly.

[
10
]

The procedure to follow under a
Rule 129(1)(a) Application is set out in a number of cases including
Tottrup
v. Alberta (Minister of Environmental Protection)
,
2000 ABCA 121 (CanLII)
,
[2000] A.J. No. 435
(C.A.)
. No evidence is to be considered on a Rule 129(1)(a) Application.

At para. 9 the Court stated:

Although
the pleadings should be liberally interpreted, the Court has a duty to apply
the Rule as it is intended. If the alleged facts examined in light of the
existing law do not disclose a cause of action then the claim should be struck.
Needless litigation should be avoided.

And at para. 13:

It
is an appropriate function of the Court to consider and determine  these
questions of law on the basis of the alleged facts. The existence of a duty of
care for example may depend on the facts of the case, but whether certain facts
can sustain a finding of such a duty is a question of law.

[
11
]

The Defendant is entitled to a
broad reading of the pleadings. The facts alleged in the Counterclaim must be
assumed to be true and capable of proof at trial.
Korte v. Deloitte,
Haskins & Sells

(1993),
1993 ABCA 78 (CanLII)
,
135 A.R. 389 (C.A.)
.

[
12
]

Does the Counterclaim disclose a
cause of action? Sana alleged that the statement discloses a number of causes
of action.

A)        Duty of Care

of the Plaintiff to Sana?

[
13
]

In the proposed amendment to the
Counterclaim Sana alleges in paragraph 4 that the Plaintiff:
“owes a
professional Duty of Care to Sana not to act in a manner that is detrimental to
the best interests of students, the public or teaching profession
” and in
paragraph 5 alleges that the Plaintiff has breached her duty of care to Sana

“by failing to respect the dignity and rights of the Defendant and her children
.”

[
14
]

The Counterclaim does not name the
children, and there are no damages claimed on behalf of the children. Sana is
essentially alleging a duty of care is owed to her by the Plaintiff as a parent
with students in attendance at the school

[
15
]

Is there a duty of care to a
parent? Counsel for the Plaintiff conceded that there are no cases to support
the duty that is being alleged. In fact several cases have specifically found
that there is not a duty owed by a teacher or administrator to a parent. For
example, in
Angle v. Lapierre
(18 October 2002), Edmonton 0203
10914 (Alta. Q.B.), Madam Justice Read was faced with similar claims against
teachers alleging a duty owed to parents and breaches of that duty. After
reviewing the law in the area she concluded at pp. 25-26 that there is no duty
of care owed to parents by teachers and that educational malpractice is not a
cause of action in Canada:

These
are claims that assert a duty that I am not prepared to find exists, at law, to
parents by teachers. Again, the claim seeks to establish duties in teachers and
administrators that are difficult to measure and vague. It is not, and should
not be, the function of the Courts to establish standards of conduct for
teachers in these matters. These are issues that teachers and administrators
can, and must, be given the opportunity to decide for themselves and nothing
has been said in the counterclaim that alleges conduct by the applicants in making
these decisions that is so egregious as to establish a cause of action.

[
16
]

While there is a duty of care
existing between teachers and students there is no connection that would extend
that duty to individual parents. In
L.R. v. British Columbia
,
1998 CanLII 3957 (BC SC)
,
[1998]
B.C.J. No. 2588 (B.C.S.C.)
, the Court expressly distinguished between a
fiduciary duty allegedly owed to students and the fiduciary duty allegedly owed
to other family members at paras. 37-38:

It
is important to distinguish the fiduciary duty allegedly owed to students from
that allegedly owed to parents and others. Based on the case law, it is
certainly arguable that the defendant owed a fiduciary duty to the students...

However,
the relationship between the government and family members as disclosed by the
pleadings is completely lacking in any of the essential ingredients necessary
to found a fiduciary relationship, and most particularly, does not disclose the
elements of discretion; influence over interests; and inherent vulnerability.

[
17
]

In the
Tottrup
case
the Alberta Court of Appeal emphasized that mere allegations of a duty are not
enough. It is necessary to look at the alleged facts and any applicable
statutes to see if the duty exists. The facts alleged to support the alleged
breach of this duty of care are:

1.         Banning Sana from the school;

2.         Sana being unable to assist her children as
a result of the ban;

3.         Reporting Sana’s behaviour to the School
Board officials;

4.         Not permitting Sana to attend her son’s
grade 6 graduation ceremony;

5.         Failing to adequately and properly consider
Sana’s concerns regarding her son’s allergies.

[
18
]

The no trespass ban was issued by
the Plaintiff in June 2004 pursuant to
Section 27
of the
School Act
as a
result of a number of incidents involving Sana. Section 27 states:

Prohibited
activities

27(1)    No person shall

(a)        disturb or interrupt the proceedings of a
school,

(b)        disturb or interrupt the proceedings of a
school meeting or board meeting, or

(c)        loiter or trespass in a school building or
on property owned by a board.

(2)    No person shall canvass, sell or offer to
sell goods, services or merchandise to a teacher or a student in a school
without the prior approval of the board.

Protection
from liability

144.1(1)            Trustees, employees of a board and
school council members are not liable for any loss or damage caused by anything
said or done or omitted to be done in good faith in the performance or intended
performance of their functions, duties or powers under this Act or any other
enactment.

(3)           Subsections (1) and (2) do not
provide a defence if the cause of action is defamation.

(4)           This section does not affect
the legal liability of a board.

[
19
]

Section 27
of the
School Act

permitted the Plaintiff as a school principal to ban people from being on
school property for nuisance reasons. Section 144.1 protects an employee who
does anything under the Act in good faith in the performance of their duties.

[
20
]

The substance of the allegation in
the Counterclaim is that Sana has a right to be present in the school and that
right was violated by the ban. There is no support  for the proposition that
Sana has an unlimited right to be on school property. In fact
Section 27
confirms
that a parent can be banned. Furthermore, there are no facts to support any
suggestion that the
section 27
ban was illegal or carried out in any way other
than in good faith. The fact that Sana was prevented from entering  the school
or from being involved in her children’s activities on school property after
being legally banned under
Section 27
of the
School Act
does not provide
a foundation for a claim of damages by statute or otherwise.

[
21
]

A similar claim is made against
the School Board relating to the ban that it issued. There are no facts to
support a suggestion that this ban was illegal or not carried out in good
faith. That claim cannot be maintained for the same reasons.

[
22
]

The other facts pleaded to support
an allegation of the existence and breach of a duty relate to an alleged

failure
to adequately and properly consider Sana’s concerns regarding her son’s
allergies, and reporting her behaviour to School Board officials.

[
23
]

As pointed out by Madam Justice
Read in
Angle
, the categories of negligence are not closed and
one must consider novel duties of care.
The Supreme Court of Canada in
Cooper
v. Hobart
,
2001 SCC 79 (CanLII)
,
[2001] 3 S.C.R. 537
clarified the analysis to be undertaken
in determining whether a duty of care should be recognized in any particular
situation. This was summarised by Mr. Justice Clackson in
Bowes v. City
of Edmonton

(2005),
2005 ABQB 502 (CanLII)
,
386 A.R. 1 (Q.B.)
at para.
92
:

The
analysis may be stated as follows:

(a)        the process involves a two stage analysis;

(b)        the first stage requires consideration of
two issues;

(c)        the first issue is whether the harm that
occurred was a reasonably foreseeable consequence of the defendant’s act;

(d)        the second issue is proximity;

(e)        proximity can be found if the defendant was
in a close and direct relationship with the plaintiff such that it is just to
impose a duty of care on that defendant in relation to that plaintiff;

(f)        alternatively, proximity can be established
if it has previously been found in a category of cases which encompasses the
same or an analogous situation as the case being considered;

(g)        if foreseeability and proximity are
established, a prima facie duty of care arises;

(h)        the second stage of the analysis requires
consideration of whether there are residual policy considerations, outside of
the relationship of the particular plaintiff and defendant, which negate
imposing a duty of care in such circumstances

(i)         where the duty of care asserted falls
within a recognized category of recovery, the court would generally be
satisfied that there are no overriding policy considerations that would
negative the duty of care.

(j)         residual policy considerations may
include:

(i)         the effect of recognizing a duty of care
on other legal obligations, the legal system, and society generally;

(ii)        whether the law already provides a remedy;

(iii)       whether recognizing a duty of care would
create unlimited liability to an unlimited class;

(iv)       whether finding a duty of care would amount
to imposing an obligation on legislators for policy decisions where to do so
would amount to second guessing the policy decisions of those legislators;

(k)        in the event that residual policy
considerations are such that imposing a duty of care would be unwise, the duty
of care will not be imposed.

[
24
]

In this case even though the
Plaintiff as a school principal and the School Board might reasonably have
foreseen that losses or harm to a parent could result from them carrying out
their duties under the
School Act

there is insufficient proximity
between the parent and the Plaintiff and School Board to ground a primary duty
of care. While the alleged harm (not being able to help her children on school
property after the ban) might be said to be forseeable, there are policy
reasons why such a duty should not be recognised. It would significantly
undermine the ability of school officials to manage schools and where necessary
to ban individuals from school property under
section 27
of the
School Act
for
safety and other reasons. The decision to ban under the
School Act
requires
a balance between public and private interests and protects anybody acting, as
in this case, in good faith.

[
25
]

In addition there is doubt in this
case as to whether any harm actually occurred, or whether or not the nature of
the alleged harm falls below the threshold of conduct for which the law
provides a remedy and is therefore
de minimis
. The allegations that
Sana’s daughter injured her knee playing basketball and Sana was unable to
assist (with no suggestion that teachers and other people present did not
provide adequate assistance), or that her son left school, slipped on a
sidewalk and had to crawl to her vehicle while she was unable to help him are
not of the nature of “harm” that should draw the protection of a duty of care.

[
26
]

These alleged facts are
de
minimis
. No injuries or damages could be reasonably based on these facts.
They do not attract any legal liability. As a result, in addition to being
struck under Rule 129(1)(a) the Plaintiff’s action  should also be struck under
Rule 129(1)(b) as lacking a legal basis and any legal merit, so as to amount to
being scandalous, frivolous and vexatious within the meaning of Rule 129(1)(b)
(
see
Borsato v. Basra
,
2000 BCSC 28 (CanLII)
,
[2000] B.C.J. No. 84 (B.C.S.C.)
;
Prefontaine
v. Gosman
,

[2000] A.J. No. 307 (Q.B.)
; and
Weisgerber v.
Weisgerber
,
2003 ABQB 763
).

B)         Defamation Claim against the Plaintiff and
the School Board.

[
27
]

Sana alleges in the Amended Counterclaim
that the Plaintiff and the School Board defamed her by making allegations to
Children’s Services. This part of the Counterclaim should be struck for the
following reasons. There is no evidentiary basis to support it. The
Counterclaim does not identify the Plaintiff or the School Board as being the
party who made the allegations. The Plaintiff is unaware of the allegations
made to Children’s Services, and they apparently involve others who are not
parties to the action.

[
28
]

Under Section 126.1 of the
Child,
Youth and Family Enhancement Act
, R.S.A. 2000, c. C-12, the name of a
person who makes the report under the
Act
is in any event privileged
information and not admissible in evidence in this action or any other. Since
the person who made the report cannot be identified, that portion of the
Counterclaim should be struck. Section 126.1 reads:

Privileged
information

126.1(1)            Despite section 126(1), the name
of a person who makes a report to the director under section 4 or 5 and
information that would identify that person is privileged information of the
person making the report and is not admissible in evidence in any action or
proceeding before any court or an Appeal Panel or before any inquiry without
the consent of the person.

(2)           Despite subsection (1), the
Minister may direct the release of information under subsection (1) that would
identify the person.

(3)           If there is a conflict or
inconsistency between subsection (1) and the
Freedom of Information and
Protection of Privacy Act
, subsection (1) prevails.

[
29
]

In summary the facts alleged in
the Counterclaim do not support a cause of action in defamation.

C)        Claim of abuse of Public Authority

against the Plaintiff and the School Board.

[
30
]

Sana asserts a claim for abuse of
public authority against both the Plaintiff and the School Board. The basis for
the claim is the trespass bans imposed under
Section 27
of the
School Act

by the Plaintiff and the School Board. The bans were made pursuant to a
statutory authority. There are no facts to support a claim that the bans were
illegal or carried out in bad faith. There is statutory protection for a party
who issues a Section 27 ban. The fact that the Plaintiff and the School Board
issued these bans without more cannot support a claim of abuse of public
authority.

D)         Claims of Discrimination and Harassment

[
31
]

Sana alleges that by banning
Sana from its property, the Board has breached its duty of care pursuant to the

School Act
and the
Human Rights, Citizenship & Multiculturalism
Act
not to discriminate with regard to services, accommodation or
facilities and that the Board breached its duty of confidentiality pursuant to
the
Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act
, R.S.A. 2000,
c. F-25. Breach of statutory duty is not actionable:
Saskatchewan Wheat
Pool v. Canada
,
1983 CanLII 21 (SCC)
,
[1983] 1 S.C.R. 205
, cited in
Guccione v.
Veterinary Medical Assn
.
(1997),
1997 CanLII 24665 (AB QB)
,
207 A.R. 331 (Q.B.)
at para.
11
.

[
32
]

The Supreme Court of Canada has
held that allegations of discrimination are not causes of action that can
support a civil action. Rather such complaints must be made pursuant to the
relevant Human Rights legislation.
Board of Governors of Seneca College
of Applied Arts and Technology v. Bhadauria
,
1981 CanLII 29 (SCC)
,
[1981] 2 S.C.R. 181
; and
Kirk
v. Prairie Bible Institute
,

[1995] A.J. No. 751 (Q.B.)
.

[
33
]

Harassment by itself is not a
cause of action: see
Bogden v. Purolator Courier Ltd.,

1996 CanLII 10572 (AB QB)
,
[1996]
A.J. No. 289 (Q.B.)
.

[
34
]

The allegations in the Human
Rights complaint are the same as those set out in Sana’s Statement of Claim. To
allow Sana to litigate these matters in two concurrent forms is an abuse of
process.

[
35
]

These allegations of
discrimination and harassment are also vague and unsubstantiated. They are
unrelated to the action for defamation and to permit such allegations to be
litigated in this action would prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial of
this action. As such they should be struck under Rule 129(1)(d) as an abuse of
process.

Conclusion on Counterclaim

[
36
]

In summary the Counterclaim in both
its original form and as amended does not in its entirety disclose a cause of
action and should be struck pursuant to Rule 129(1)(a) and (b).

Issue # 2:         Should the Affidavit filed by Sana
in support of the application to amend the Counterclaim be struck?

[
37
]

The Plaintiff seeks to have the
Affidavit(s) filed by Sana in support of the application to add the ATA and
amend the Counterclaim struck on the basis they are vexatious and scandalous.

[
38
]

The rules relating to the contents
of affidavits are Rules 305, 306 and 307:

Facts and belief

305(1)   Affidavits shall be confined to the statement
of facts within the knowledge of the deponent.

(2)  In an action or proceeding to which a
corporation is a party any affidavit required by these Rules to be made by a
party may be made by an officer, servant or agent of the corporation having
knowledge of the facts required to be deposed to, who shall state therein that
he has that knowledge.

(3)  On interlocutory motions affidavits
containing statements as to the belief of the deponent with the source and
grounds thereof may be admitted.

Irregularity
of form

306       An affidavit may, with the leave of the
Court, be filed or used in evidence notwithstanding any irregularity in the
form thereof.

Striking
out matter

307       The Court may order to be struck out of any
affidavit any matter which is scandalous, irrelevant or otherwise oppressive.

[
39
]

A review of Sana’s affidavit dated
October 13, 2006 indicates that a number of paragraphs do not comply with the
Rules
of Court
. For example, Paragraphs 3, 4, 9, 10 and 13 offend Rule 305(1) as
they do not contain facts but rather contain arguments and assertions. Many of
these paragraphs also offend Rule 307 as they contain matters irrelevant to the
issues in the action.

[
40
]

As it is not practical to remove
the offending material the affidavit should be struck from the record.

ISSUE #3:         Should the ATA be added as a party
to the Counterclaim
?

[
41
]

Sana seeks to add the Alberta
Teachers Association as a Defendant to the Counterclaim. The reasons for doing
so are not that clear. Sana alleges that the ATA has somehow prejudged her. In
addition it is suggested that the Plaintiff’s legal costs are being covered by
the ATA.

[
42
]

The ATA and the Plaintiff oppose
the application. They note that this defamation action is a personal action.
The action does not allege that Sana defamed the ATA. The evidence is that
there is no involvement by the ATA in this action other than to provide member
services to the Plaintiff. Even if those member services include the ATA paying
the teacher’s legal costs, that is no
basis to add the ATA as a party:
Angle v. Lapierre
,
[2006] A.J.
No.618 (Q.B.) at paras. 6-10
.

[
43
]

The application to
add the ATA as a party is dismissed.

Issue #4:         Should
paragraphs 22 and 23 of the Amended statement of claim be struck
?

[
44
]

Paragraphs 22 and 23 of the
Amended Statement of Claim state as follows:

22.        On or about September 10, 2004, having
obtained Sana’s verbal confirmation that Sana would abide by the parameters set
for the mediation and would attend the mediation with Mr. Sana, the mediator
arranged for by Edmonton Public Schools, Sharon Wilson of Resources
International (“Wilson”) met with Sana and Elkow. Mr. Sana failed or refused to
attend. At the mediation meeting, Sana refused to sign a facilitation agreement
to work in good faith and to keep the discussions confidential between the
parties, then published more threats and accusations, inter alia that Elkow
abused Samina, that Elkow discriminated against Sana for wearing a head scarf,
that Sana would call the media, human rights, and the Court, and would sue
Elkow and get her fired, and that “the world would know that Elkow was an
unqualified principal”, or words to that effect. Sana also said to Wilson and
Elkow that Sana’s best friend has children attending another school operated by
Edmonton Public Schools, and that school also had a Jewish principal who was
dishonest and discriminated against female Muslims with headscarves, or words
to that effect. Sana also said to Wilson and Elkow that Elkow had turned
teachers against Sana and caused the Sana children to decline in academic
standing, or words to that effect, Sana also said to Wilson and Elkow that she
hated Elkow and could never forgive her for what Elkow had done to her, or
words to that effect. Sana also said to Wilson and Elkow that she (Sana) talks
about her issues with Elkow to everyone she can because that allows her to
share her pain and to feel better, or words to that effect.

23.        Sana’s statements and demeanor at the
meeting with Wilson and Elkow on or about September 10, 2004, were so angry and
unrelenting that Wilson expressed fears for Elkow’s and her safety and
accompanied Elkow to her car after the meeting. Thereafter, Sana called Wilson
to scream hysterical accusations against Elkow in such manner and to such
extent that Wilson called the School and expressed her concerns about the
safety of Elkow and others in the School.

[
45
]

Sana alleges that these paragraphs
refer to a mediation process that took place between the parties. The mediation
was intended to be an off the record meeting and that as such there is
privilege attached to the meeting. The Plaintiff and the School Board
acknowledge that there was an attempt at mediation but it never got underway as
Sana refused to sign the confidentiality agreement and agree to the ground
rules of the mediation.

[
46
]

I accept the evidence that while a
mediation was planned it never started as Sana refused to agree to the rules of
the process. As a result there is no privilege attached to this interaction
between the parties. The application to strike these paragraphs is dismissed.
